R02-E-01: The line-judgement experiments of the 1950s are among the most retold stories in psychology, and the moral usually drawn from them is a gloomy one. A participant sits among strangers who, one after another, give an obviously wrong answer about which of several lines matches a standard; when the participant's turn comes, he often repeats their error. The lesson, we are told, is that ordinary people will deny the evidence of their own eyes rather than stand apart from a crowd. This reading has become so familiar that it is easy to forget how much interpretation it smuggles in. Begin with the numbers that the gloomy version tends to leave out. On the critical trials, most of the answers participants gave were correct, and a sizeable share of people never yielded at all. A study that is remembered as a demonstration of conformity could as easily be remembered as a demonstration of independence under strange and uncomfortable conditions. Which of these stories gets told says more about the teller than about the data. More important is the question of what yielding meant. Outside the laboratory, when several people who seem competent and sincere all report the same thing, the rational response is to give their reports considerable weight, even against one's own impression. Our senses err, and other people are among the best instruments we have for catching their errors. A participant who reasoned, 'I cannot see why they are all saying this, but it is unlikely that every one of them is mistaken,' was not abandoning reason; he was applying a rule that serves well almost everywhere except in a room deliberately arranged to defeat it. On this view much of what looks like spineless deference is better described as informational influence: treating others as evidence. None of this means that the pressure in the room was imaginary. Variations in which participants wrote their answers privately, rather than announcing them aloud, produced far less agreement with the majority, which suggests that some yielding was about avoiding embarrassment rather than about belief. Participants interviewed afterwards also described acute discomfort, and some admitted that they had answered against what they saw. Normative pressure, the wish to fit in, was real. The point is not that it was absent but that it was only part of the picture, and that collapsing everything into it produces a caricature. The caricature matters because it shapes the remedies we prescribe. If people conform because they are weak, the cure is to exhort them to be brave. If they conform partly because they are sensibly using others as sources of information, the cure is better information: making dissent visible, so that a single honest voice breaks the appearance of unanimity, and designing institutions in which the reasons behind a majority view can be inspected rather than merely counted.
R02-E-02: Few findings in social psychology have escaped the laboratory as completely as the bystander effect. In its popular form it says that the more people witness an emergency, the less likely the victim is to receive help, and it is usually offered as evidence of modern apathy: crowds of onlookers, each waiting for someone else to act. The idea owes much of its fame to a newspaper account of a murder in a city street in the 1960s, in which dozens of neighbours were said to have watched and done nothing. Later investigation suggested that the account greatly exaggerated both the number of witnesses and their indifference, but by then the story had become a parable. The experiments that followed were more careful than the parable. Their central claim was not that people are callous but that responsibility, when shared, is diluted. A person who believes that she alone has heard a cry for help knows that if she does not act, no one will; a person who knows that others have heard it can reasonably suppose that someone better placed is already responding. Ambiguity compounds the effect. In a group, each witness looks to the others to work out whether anything is really wrong, and the calm faces of people who are themselves only watching can persuade everyone that nothing is. Yet there is a gap between what these studies measured and what the popular version claims. They showed that a given individual is less likely to help when others are present. They did not show that a victim is less likely to be helped. The two come apart because a crowd contains many potential helpers: even if each one is somewhat less willing, the chance that at least one of them steps forward can remain high, and may rise as the crowd grows. Some recent studies of recorded conflicts in public places have reported that in most of them at least one bystander intervened, a pattern hard to reconcile with the image of the paralysed crowd. None of this makes the original research worthless. The mechanisms it identified are real, and they help explain why emergencies in which no one is sure what is happening, or whose job it is to act, can go unanswered. What it does not support is a sweeping verdict on human nature. The practical advice that follows from the research is modest and useful: if you need help, single out one person and tell that person what to do, so that responsibility is no longer shared and the situation is no longer ambiguous.
R02-E-03: Imagine being told, after a brief task in which you estimated the number of dots flashed on a screen, that you belong to the group of 'overestimators'. You never meet another member of your group; you do not know who they are; nothing hangs on the label. You are then asked to divide small sums of money between two anonymous people, one described as an overestimator and the other as an underestimator. Experiments built on this design, which came to be called the minimal group paradigm, found that people reliably gave a little more to members of their own arbitrary category. Some even preferred allocations that maximised the gap between the groups over allocations that would have given their own group more in absolute terms. The result has often been read as a revelation about human nature. If a meaningless label is enough to produce favouritism, the argument runs, then tribalism must be wired into us, waiting for any pretext, and the deeper divisions of nation, religion and ethnicity are only this primitive tendency writ large. The reading is dramatic, but it outruns the evidence in two ways. First, what the experiments mostly showed was favouritism, not hostility. Participants tilted rewards towards their own side, but they were generally reluctant to impose costs on the other side when the task was framed as distributing penalties rather than rewards. Giving one's own a little more is not the same as wishing the others harm, and a theory of intergroup conflict that treats the two as interchangeable will misunderstand both. Second, the favouritism itself may be less mindless than it looks. Several later studies suggested that it shrinks when participants are told that members of their group will not know how they allocated, as though people were partly acting on an expectation that their own side would reciprocate. On that account the label is not a trigger for blind loyalty but a cue about whom one is in a cooperative relationship with. None of this makes the original finding trivial. It remains striking that so thin a basis for belonging should shape behaviour at all, and the speed with which people adopt a category as their own deserves to be taken seriously. But the lesson that follows is not the fatalistic one. If group membership can be conjured from a coin toss or a dot-counting task, then it can also be redrawn: categories that are learned so easily are not fixed, and identities that cut across existing divisions can be built by the same mechanism that builds divisions in the first place. What the laboratory cannot tell us is why particular divisions in the world become bitter. Real groups have histories, grievances and competing claims on land, jobs and power, and a five-minute label carries none of these. The minimal group paradigm shows where the raw material of loyalty comes from; it does not show what turns that material into enmity.
R02-E-04: Empathy enjoys a reputation that few other psychological capacities can match. To be told that one lacks it is an accusation; to call for more of it is to sound wise. Yet if empathy is understood in its strict sense, as the capacity to feel what another person feels, to be distressed by their distress and buoyed by their relief, there are reasons to doubt that it is a dependable guide to how we ought to act, however much it enriches how we live. The trouble lies in its shape. Empathy works like a narrow beam: it illuminates whatever it is pointed at with great intensity and leaves everything else in darkness. It is most easily directed at people who are near us, who resemble us and who can be seen as individuals with faces and names. It is notoriously insensitive to number; the plight of one child described in detail can move us more than a report of thousands suffering in the same way, because thousands cannot be felt, only counted. A capacity with these properties will reliably favour the identifiable over the statistical, the familiar over the strange and the present over the future, and those are precisely the biases that moral reasoning is supposed to correct. There is a darker possibility as well. Because empathy is felt for particular victims, it can be recruited against other people. An account of a single person wronged by a member of some group can stir a fierce sympathy that is then turned into demands for punishment of the whole group. The emotion in such cases is genuine; what is wrong is its range. The obvious objection is that without empathy we would not care at all, and that a morality built only on principle would be bloodless. But this assumes that empathy is the only route to concern. Many people help strangers without imagining their way into the strangers' experience, out of a settled wish that others fare well, a sense of fairness, or the plain recognition that suffering is bad wherever it occurs. Psychologists sometimes distinguish empathy from compassion along these lines: the first means sharing another's feeling, the second means caring about another's good without necessarily sharing the feeling. Compassion, unlike empathic distress, does not exhaust the carer, and it can be extended to people one will never see. None of this is an argument for coldness. In friendship, in parenting and in the consulting room, the ability to feel with another person is part of what makes the relationship what it is, and nobody would wish it away. The claim is narrower: that when we must decide how to allocate help across many people, or how to treat those we do not know, a feeling that shines only where it is pointed should be checked by judgement rather than trusted as the measure of what is right.
R02-E-05: Why should anyone help a stranger they will never meet again? Kindness between relatives can be explained by shared interests, and kindness between neighbours by the expectation that favours will be returned. But much of human cooperation takes place between people who are neither kin nor repeat partners: the traveller who returns a lost wallet, the customer who corrects an undercharge. One influential answer is that such acts are paid for not by the person helped but by everyone who comes to hear of them. If people prefer to help those who have a record of helping others, then a good reputation is an asset, and an act of generosity towards a stranger is an investment in it. Biologists call this arrangement indirect reciprocity. The idea has an obvious weakness, and its defenders have had to work hard to answer it. Reputation is only as useful as the information that carries it. In a small band where everyone watches everyone, deeds are seen and remembered; in a large society most of them go unwitnessed. Here language does decisive work. Gossip, often dismissed as idle, is the channel through which a person's conduct becomes known to people who never saw it, and a great deal of everyday conversation consists of exactly this exchange of judgements about absent third parties. Without such talk, indirect reciprocity could hardly operate beyond the scale of a village. A subtler problem concerns the judgements themselves. Suppose I refuse to help someone who is known to cheat. Should observers count my refusal against me? If they do, anyone who withholds help from cheats will be punished for it, and cheating becomes safer. If they do not, observers must keep track not only of what people did but of whom they did it to and why. Models of indirect reciprocity suggest that cooperation is far more stable under the second, more demanding standard, which may help explain why people care so much about motives and context when they assess one another's behaviour. It would be too much to say that reputation explains all cooperation among strangers. People sometimes behave generously in conditions of genuine anonymity, and laboratory attempts to show that subtle cues of being watched, such as pictures of eyes, make people more generous have produced mixed results. A defender of the reputational account can reply that habits formed in a world where anonymity was rare are not switched off merely because a particular situation happens to be unobserved. That reply is plausible, but it shifts the explanation from calculation to disposition, and it should be acknowledged as a shift. What survives is a narrower and more defensible claim: that the expectation of being talked about is one of the main forces that make large-scale cooperation possible, and that it works only as well as the talk is accurate.
R02-E-06: For a time it was widely believed, among journalists and fact-checkers as much as among researchers, that correcting a false belief could make matters worse. The idea, which came to be called the backfire effect, held that people confronted with evidence against a cherished belief would not merely resist it but cling to the belief more tightly, as though the correction were an attack to be repelled. It had an intuitive appeal: most of us have argued with someone who seemed to grow more certain with every fact we offered. And it carried a discouraging moral. If correction backfires, perhaps it is better not to correct at all. Subsequent research has been considerably kinder to correction. Larger studies, with more varied topics and more diverse participants, have generally found that people who receive a factual correction move, on average, towards the accurate view, even when the correction cuts against their political loyalties. Reversal of the kind the early findings described appears to be rare, and some of the original results have proved difficult to reproduce. The more careful conclusion is not that people are perfectly responsive to evidence but that they are responsive to it in the ordinary, imperfect way: they update, though often less than they should. It is worth asking why the backfire idea spread so far on so slender a basis. Part of the answer is that it flattered a certain cynicism about the public, and part is that it confused resistance with reversal. Someone who hears a correction and does not change his mind has resisted it; someone who becomes more convinced of the falsehood has reversed. The first is common and unremarkable, since people rarely abandon a belief after a single encounter with contrary evidence. Only the second would justify the conclusion that correcting is counterproductive, and it is the second that the evidence has failed to find with any regularity. This does not mean that correction is a cure. Its effects often fade over weeks, so that people drift back towards the belief they were talked out of, and accepting that a particular claim is false does not necessarily change the attitudes the claim was used to support. A voter may concede that a politician's statistic was wrong and still admire the politician exactly as much. These are serious limits, but they are limits of a different kind. They call for corrections that are repeated, that offer an alternative explanation rather than a bare denial, and that are not expected to carry more weight than a single fact can bear. They do not call for silence. The history of the backfire effect is thus a small lesson about the life of findings as well as about belief. A striking result, especially one that confirms what people already suspect, can travel much faster than the slower work of checking it, and the effort to correct a mistaken finding meets the same ordinary resistance, though not reversal, that greets any correction.
R02-E-07: In most human groups some people are listened to more than others, get their way more often and receive a larger share of whatever the group values. Students of status have long suspected that this single word conceals two different arrangements. In one, a person rises because others fear him: he can hurt them, withhold what they need or make their lives difficult, and they defer in order to avoid those costs. In the other, a person rises because others want something from him that he gives freely, usually knowledge or skill, and they defer in order to stay close enough to learn. The first route is commonly called dominance and the second prestige, and an influential line of thought in evolutionary anthropology holds that the second is a distinctively human addition to an older primate inheritance. The argument for that view rests on the peculiar importance of cultural learning in our species. A creature that acquires most of its survival skills by copying others faces a constant problem of whom to copy, and a strong incentive to secure access to the best models. Deference, on this account, is a kind of payment: the learner offers attention, praise, small services and a willingness to yield in disputes, and in return is tolerated at the elbow of the skilled. If the account is right, it explains why prestige is freely conferred rather than extracted, why prestigious people are approached rather than avoided, and why we find ourselves imitating not only what admired people do well but much else about them besides. That last consequence deserves more attention than it usually receives, because it shows that prestige is not simply the benign twin of dominance. Imitation guided by prestige is broad and indiscriminate. A learner cannot always tell which of a successful person's habits are responsible for the success, and so tends to copy a bundle of them: the method, but also the dress, the opinions and the manner of speech. In a small community this overspill is cheap and may even be useful, since the bundle often travels together for good reasons. In a large society with mass media, it allows people who are prestigious in one domain to exert influence far outside it, and the deference they receive bears no relation to any competence they have in the matters on which they are now heeded. There is a further complication. The two routes are clean in theory and tangled in practice. A person who gains prestige acquires allies, resources and a following, and these are exactly the instruments with which dominance is exercised; prestige can thus be converted into the power to coerce, and the conversion is not always visible to those who continue to admire. Conversely, a dominant figure may cultivate the outward marks of prestige, surrounding himself with displays of learning or generosity that make submission feel like admiration. Observers who ask simply whether a leader is feared or respected will often find that the honest answer is both. None of this undermines the distinction; it is precisely because the two routes can be told apart in principle that their mixture in practice becomes something to look for. What it undermines is the comfortable assumption that a society which replaces dominance with prestige has thereby solved the problem of status. Prestige allocates influence according to perceived excellence, and perception can be managed. The practical question for any institution is therefore not whether it rewards prestige rather than force, which most modern institutions at least claim to do, but whether it keeps the deference people receive tied to the domain in which they have actually earned it.
R02-E-08: Few episodes have shaken social psychology as much as the attempts, over roughly the past decade and a half, to repeat some of its best-known experiments. Among the findings that fared worst were studies of so-called behavioural priming, which reported that subtle exposure to an idea could shift what people did shortly afterwards: that reading words associated with old age made people walk more slowly down a corridor, for instance, or that being reminded of money made them less helpful. Such results were taught in lecture halls and retold in popular books. When larger and more carefully controlled attempts to reproduce several of them found effects much smaller than those first reported, or none that could be detected, the reaction within the field was bitter, and the debate quickly took on the character of a trial. That framing has not served anyone well. It invites the question of who was dishonest, when the more troubling lesson is that dishonesty was largely unnecessary. A literature can come to look robust through practices that most of the people using them regarded as normal: running small studies, trying several reasonable ways of analysing the data and reporting the one that worked, and publishing successes while filing failures away. Each practice, taken alone, seems a minor licence. Together they make it likely that a field will accumulate striking positive results whether or not the underlying effects are real, and that the most surprising results, which are the most likely to be false, will also be the most celebrated. It is important to be clear about what the failed replications do and do not show. They do not show that priming in general is an illusion. That encountering one word makes a related word easier to recognise a moment later is among the most reliable findings in the study of cognition, and nothing in the recent debate casts doubt on it. Nor does a failed repetition of a single study prove that the effect it sought is exactly zero; it shows that the effect, if it exists, is smaller or less dependable than the original report implied. The questions under dispute concern a particular, ambitious claim: that brief and incidental cues reliably steer complex social behaviour. Defenders of that claim have often replied that social behaviour is sensitive to context, so that an effect obtained with one population, in one decade, with one set of materials, need not appear when any of these is changed. There is something to this. Human beings are not inert objects, and it would be strange if the meaning of a word list were identical across cultures and generations. But the reply has a cost that its proponents do not always acknowledge. The original studies were presented as revealing general features of human minds, not as local facts about particular groups of students. If the effects are so delicate that unknown features of a setting can abolish them, then those general claims were overstated, and an appeal to hidden moderators that is made only after a failure, and never specified in advance so that it could be tested, explains everything and therefore nothing. The reforms that the episode prompted, such as registering hypotheses and analyses before collecting data and running studies large enough to detect modest effects, have costs of their own. Research becomes slower and more expensive, and fewer dazzling results will appear. That is the right trade. A science of social behaviour that publishes fewer surprises, each of which can bear weight, is worth more than one whose surprises must all be taken on trust.
